documents.abstract: Traffic safety countermeasure recommendation requires simultaneous consideration of crash context, roadway facility, traffic control, operating conditions, and evidence applicability. Traditional rule-based and keyword-matching methods have difficulty processing natural-language crash-context queries. This study proposes an evidence-grounded and mechanism-aware framework that formulates traffic safety countermeasure recommendation as the construction, selection, and ranking of CMF Evidence Cards. A structured CMF Evidence Store containing 8844 Evidence Cards was developed from the CMF Clearinghouse. A corpus of 2935 crash-context queries was further constructed, including 1935 complete queries and 1000 controlled incomplete variants. For each query, the framework constructs a candidate evidence pool through Context-aware Retrieval, Mechanism-aware Recall Augmentation, and Engineering Applicability Filtering. A large language model fine-tuned through supervised learning then selects and ranks up to three Evidence IDs and returns the corresponding countermeasure descriptions, CMF or CRF values, evidence quality, applicability conditions, and literature sources. The fine-tuned Qwen3-32B achieved an Exact Evidence Top-1 of 53.14%, an Exact Evidence Hit@3 of 76.15%, a Mechanism Hit@3 of 83.26%, an Exact Evidence Jaccard of 44.18%, and an Empty-set Decision Accuracy of 95.08%. Module-level ablation results confirmed the distinct contributions of the three candidate evidence construction components. Candidate-pool sensitivity analysis showed that evidence coverage reached saturation at approximately 30 Evidence Cards. The proposed framework also substantially outperformed a conventional BM25-RAG baseline and maintained stable performance across semantically equivalent query paraphrases. LLM-assisted and independent expert evaluations further supported the contextual relevance, mechanism consistency, engineering applicability, and overall usefulness of the recommendations. Case studies demonstrated the framework's ability to address mechanism-complex and facility-specific traffic safety scenarios, while also identifying evidence retrieval as a limitation in specialized contexts such as work zones.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents in non-verifiable domains such as financial services, where they must interpret user intent, rewrite queries, and retrieve information under domain-specific constraints. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can train such agents from the consequences of their actions, recent successes largely rely on verifiable tasks with automatically computed binary rewards. In non-verifiable retrieval tasks, assessing query quality requires scarce subject-matter expert (SME) judgment that is inherently graded rather than binary. With Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), sparse rewards yield no useful learning signal when all sampled outputs within a group receive the same outcome, causing optimization to stall. We introduce a method that converts a small, fixed investment of SME judgment into a dense reward and combines it with retrieval-based metrics to form a hybrid, GRPO-compatible training signal. Experiments show improvements of up to 6\% in Recall@3 and 6.7\% in MRR@3 compared with sparse-reward baselines.

To promote the design of low-carbon alkali-activated materials, precise yet interpretable compressive strength prediction based on mix design variables is essential to minimize trial-and-error experimentation. This study employs an interpretable machine learning approach to predict compressive strength based on important mix design variables, including fly ash content, ground granulated blast furnace slag content, Na 2 O content, SiO 2 /Na 2 O ratio and water to binder ratio. Various ensemble machine learning models, such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Decision Tree, XGBoost, and LightGBM were developed and compared for model performance evaluation using R 2 , RMSE and MAE. Among the models, the Random Forest model had the best generalization performance with a test coefficient R² of 0.762, along with RMSE of 9.23 MPa and MAE of 6.38 MPa. Explainable artificial intelligence techniques were then used to interpret the machine learning model predictions and determine the variable contributions. The results consistently showed that the water to binder ratio is the most dominant factor influencing the compressive strength, followed by Na 2 O content, fly ash content and SiO 2 /Na 2 O ratio. A clear nonlinear threshold was found at a water to binder ratio of approximately 0.5, beyond which the predicted compressive strength dropped rapidly. Therefore, the interpretable machine learning framework presented in this study minimizes trial-and-error experimentation by providing accurate compressive strength prediction and clear, mix-design-related explanations for the development of low-carbon alkali-activated materials.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming the possibilities for informal language learning by providing immediate feedback, conversational interaction, and potentially personalized learning experiences. However, its use does not necessarily entail greater learner autonomy, self-regulation, or agency. This study aimed to understand how Colombian adults configure their informal English learning practices through GenAI tools, with particular attention to decision-making processes, self-regulation, evaluation of AI-generated responses, and the articulation of GenAI with other learning resources. Adopting a qualitative, exploratory, and interpretive approach, the study involved four Colombian adults with diverse linguistic, educational, and GenAI-use trajectories. Data were generated through participant characterization forms, GenAI interaction records, semi-structured interviews, and, when available, documentary evidence of participants’ interactions with the technology. A predominantly inductive thematic analysis generated four interconnected categories: negotiating control over the learning interaction; constructing and calibrating trust in AI-generated feedback; experiencing personalization through responsive interaction; and reconfiguring the broader learning repertoire. Findings show that participants assumed, negotiated, and delegated control in different ways and developed varying criteria for accepting, questioning, or verifying GenAI-generated responses. They also selectively integrated GenAI with other digital and human learning resources. Based on these findings, the study conceptualizes GenAI appropriation as a form of situated orchestration through which learners coordinate technological affordances with their purposes, prior knowledge, evaluative criteria, and broader learning repertoires. The findings suggest that GenAI does not automatically produce learner autonomy or agency; rather, it creates new spaces in which these may be exercised, negotiated, or delegated.

The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into multilingual digital environments has raised specific questions about contextual appropriateness, sociopragmatic calibration, and interactional adaptation across culturally situated norms. While benchmarks have evaluated LLM performance across dozens of languages, these assessments remain confined to classification tasks and are not designed to assess productive sociopragmatic competence in underrepresented ecologies such as Indonesian. This study compares speech act production between three flagship LLMs (GPT-5, Claude Opus 4.1, Gemini 3 Pro) and 150 Indonesian native speakers. Data were elicited using a 16-scenario Discourse Completion Task spanning requests, refusals, complaints, and apologies across varied power (+/-P) and distance (+/-D) configurations. Responses were coded using an adapted Cross-Cultural Speech Act Realization Patterns (CCSARP) framework and digital-pragmatic categories capturing emoji, phatic markers, colloquial particles, and code-mixing characteristic of Indonesian online discourse. Results indicate that while all three LLMs produced grammatically well-formed and strategically recognisable speech acts, significant divergences emerged in face-work calibration, scalar modification, and text-based digital-pragmatic signalling. All models systematically preferred negative politeness strategies and used basa-basi (phatic communion), colloquial particles, code-mixing, and emoji less frequently, while deploying honorifics with less contextual specificity than human responses. Claude Opus 4.1 exhibited the most conservative profile, while Gemini 3 Pro showed the greatest contextual sensitivity, though all remained distinct from the Indonesian native-speaker comparison group. These findings provide an early production-based empirical comparison of LLM pragmatic alignment in Indonesian digital interaction, contributing to computational sociopragmatics with implications for AI safety, cross-cultural NLP evaluation, and sociopragmatically aware language technologies.

Introduction: Low back pain (LBP) is an important occupational health concern among dental students and practising dentists. This systematic review aimed to synthesise evidence on ergonomic and individual factors associated with LBP, distinguish directly measured findings from hypothesised biomechanical or anatomical pathways, and identify implications for multilevel occupational health promotion. Methods: This systematic review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and Google Scholar were searched for English-language studies published from 1 January 2021 through 31 May 2026. Two reviewers independently screened records and extracted data. Of 327 records identified, 24 full-text reports were assessed and 6 studies were included in a qualitative synthesis because populations, exposures, outcomes, and analytical methods were heterogeneous. Results: Six studies were included. The studies directly assessed self-reported LBP or disability, working posture, sitting duration, physical activity, age, body mass index, years of practice, and, in one study, trunk-movement parameters. Estimates from students and practising dentists were not directly comparable. Non-neutral posture and selected occupational or individual factors were associated with LBP in some studies, but findings were inconsistent for sitting duration, physical activity, and years of practice. Proposed changes in lumbar loading, alignment, or stability were not directly measured in most studies. Conclusion: Available evidence suggests associations between selected ergonomic or individual factors and LBP among dental students and practising dentists, but heterogeneous populations, predominantly cross-sectional designs, and self-reported measures limit causal inference. The findings may inform candidate occupational health-promotion actions at the individual, professional-education, work-organisation, and clinical-environment levels; however, the included studies did not evaluate their effectiveness. Prospective controlled studies are required before preventive effectiveness can be inferred.

This systematic literature review analyses factors associated with research literacy among university students based on 50 studies published between 1 January 2015 and 31 December 2025. Following PRISMA guidelines, studies were selected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Science Direct databases. The findings reveal research literacy as a multidimensional competency operating through three interconnected dimensions — personal (63%), pedagogical (23%) and institutional (14%), computed over the 35 studies with extractable quantitative data —. Personal factors showed the strongest statistical associations, with information literacy (d = 0.82) and research self-efficacy (d = 0.76) yielding the largest pooled effect sizes. Pedagogical factors, though less represented, were associated with the largest effect sizes, particularly library-faculty collaboration (d = 0.94) and structured instruction (d = 0.78). Institutional factors, including frameworks and technological resources, were consistently associated with larger estimates for personal and pedagogical variables, a pattern compatible with — but not demonstrative of — an amplifying role. The review identified a paradigmatic shift from traditional information literacy toward critical artificial intelligence literacy, with a 410% growth in AI-related studies between 2023–2025. Bibliometric analysis revealed geographical concentration in Europe and Asia (50%), highlighting underrepresentation of Global South perspectives. Methodological limitations include predominance of correlational designs (36%) and scarcity of longitudinal studies (12%). The study proposes an explanatory framework in which institutional conditions operate as contextual antecedents that shape instructional opportunity, which in turn relates to individual research competence through research self-efficacy, with discipline, academic stage and prior digital competence acting as moderators; four testable propositions are derived from it. Because the evidence base is predominantly correlational, these findings should be read as associations rather than causal effects; they provide an evidence-informed basis for designing educational strategies intended to foster critical thinking, information evaluation, and ethical research practices in contemporary higher education contexts.

Islamic boarding schools are educational institutions that focus on teaching religious knowledge, including various traditional Islamic books. Besides that, pesantren also equip students with various positive life skills, like memorizing hadiths, practicing prayer, leading prayers, and other life skills. The study aims to analyze the factors influencing the development of students' social skills at Islamic Boarding Schools. This study adopted a qualitative case study approach. The study was conducted at the Mambaul 'Ulum Tujungmuli Islamic Boarding School, Karangmoncol District, Purbalingga Regency. The subjects were the caretakers of the Islamic boarding school. Data were collected using interview and documentation techniques. Data were analyzed using interactive analysis. The results of the study reported that the development of students' life skills was influenced both driving and inhibiting factors. The driving factors originated from both internal and external sources. Internal aspects were characterized by the willingness and enthusiasm of the caretakers, the purpose of establishing the Islamic boarding school, sociological awareness, and internalization of Islamic boarding school teachings. External aspects were characterized by of the importance of deepening religious knowledge, the community's need for education, the desire to build social integration, and maintaining harmony among humans. Factors inhibiting the development of students' life skills included technological changes and changing times, a lack of communication between residents and the Islamic boarding school, limited agricultural land, and inadequate agricultural infrastructure.

Repeated users of an artificial-intelligence agent may learn both its competence and how it sounds. This paper proposes that acquired style congruence can change acceptance independently of evidential quality, while any benefit to error management may arise through more than one route. Learned style–correctness contingencies can guide classification; reduced processing demands may also free attention for substantive checking when style itself is non-diagnostic. The framework distinguishes recognition, response criterion, classification sensitivity, competence learning, defect identification, successful correction, and final accuracy. Five competing mechanisms are specified: familiarity halo, anomaly vigilance, diagnostic cue learning, competence learning, and processing-efficiency learning. Building on appropriate-reliance research, calibration symmetry is treated as a requirement for identification and measurement: both familiar-looking wrong answers and unfamiliar-looking correct answers must be examined. It does not imply equal frequency, cost, or normative importance. The contribution is a bounded synthesis for acquired, source-specific style, not a new general principle of reliance or a demonstrated familiarity effect. Study 1 crosses acquired style congruence with correctness while preserving randomized assignment and measuring inferred source or version change. Study 2 varies cue diagnosticity and distinguishes classification through style from identifying and repairing substantive defects. Outcome feedback, trial-level learning, delayed unaided performance, and transfer are specified separately from assisted performance. Conversational affirmation and linguistic accommodation are adjacent pathways, not evidence of acquired-style effects. Governance implications remain provisional pending direct evidence.

The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) has become a fundamental component of modern industrial automation by connecting sensors, actuators, programmable logic controllers, robotic systems, machines, edge devices, and cloud platforms for continuous monitoring and intelligent control. However, the dependence of industrial operations on interconnected IoT networks introduces significant risks associated with communication failures, sensor faults, hardware degradation, software errors, cyber-attacks, congestion, and edge computing failures. A single failure can interrupt production, reduce product quality, increase maintenance costs, or create safety hazards. This paper examines the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve fault tolerance in IoT networks used for industrial automation. The paper reviews recent developments in AI based fault detection, anomaly detection, predictive maintenance, intelligent routing, and edge based recovery, and adaptive resource management. Recent studies demonstrate that machine learning can identify abnormal device and sensor behavior before failures propagate, while Software Defined Networking can support rapid route restoration and network recovery. AI enabled edge computing further reduces response latency by moving fault analysis closer to industrial devices. The paper proposes a conceptual AI enabled fault tolerant architecture consisting of an IoT sensing layer, resilient communication layer, edge intelligence layer, AI fault analysis layer, decision and recovery layer, and industrial control layer. The proposed approach combines real-time monitoring, machine-learning-based prediction, redundant communication paths, automated recovery, and predictive maintenance. The paper concludes that integrating AI with fault-tolerance mechanisms can improve industrial network availability, reliability, resilience, and operational continuity. Nevertheless, challenges involving data quality, explain ability, computational resources, cyber security, interoperability, and validation in real industrial environments require further investigation.

documents.abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. A phone's neural processing unit (NPU) already holds these weights for inference; using it for training also requires computing input gradients, which its inference interface does not support. We present a system that runs all three frozen-weight products on the NPU while keeping the training graph, adapters, and optimizer on the CPU. Its input-gradient kernels reuse the resident weight tiles and the forward dequantizer, avoiding a transposed weight copy and ensuring forward and backward use the same effective weights. To preserve usable gradients, the system selects precision by gradient sensitivity and applies a per-row range guard for half-precision (FP16) outputs. Its runtime fuses the remaining CPU operators and overlaps NPU execution with adapter computation, while resumable execution and thermal pacing let training proceed as a background job. We evaluate it on two Qualcomm Snapdragon platforms using four LLMs from the Qwen and Llama families. Our workloads cover nightly personalization with labels supplied on the phone and the public LaMP-2 benchmark; comparisons include an optimized CPU trainer, a phone-GPU trainer, forward-only training, and GPU-trained references.

Generative AI workflows execute user tasks by composing sequences of LLM calls, where each call performs a sub-task (e.g., summarization or translation), forming a workflow. Executing such workflows requires decisions over workflow structure, model assignments, and deployment configurations, which jointly determine latency, cost, and accuracy under dynamic workloads and resource constraints. Existing systems optimize these decisions in isolation or fix them early, leading to suboptimal cost and goodput. We make two key observations. First, efficient serving requires jointly exploring all combinations of workflows, model choices, and deployment configurations under dynamic cluster state. Second, reuse of deployed LLMs is critical for reducing cost, but must be performed on-the-fly, as reuse depends on current load and resource availability. Together, these make selecting a workflow-variant-a combination of workflow, models, and deployment configuration-a time-critical problem. We present FlowMaker, which exposes a task-level interface and selects workflow-variants on behalf of users. To realize this, we design a constraint-guided load-aware pruning algorithm for fast, on-the-fly decisions. FlowMaker improves goodput by up to 10.14$\times$ and reduces cost by up to 2.77$\times$ compared to state-of-the-art baselines, including Murakkab.

Abstract Whether students develop dependence on generative artificial intelligence (AI) technologies largely depends on their attitudes toward using such tools. Existing studies have primarily explained the formation of AI dependence from the perspectives of usage attitudes and technological characteristics, while paying limited attention to the psychological mechanisms through which attitudes exert their influence. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, the present study examines how different types of use motivation mediate the relationship between students’ AI attitudes and AI dependence. A total of 405 university students completed a comprehensive questionnaire measuring AI attitudes, use motivations, and AI dependence. The results indicate that: (i) AI attitudes do not directly predict AI dependence; instead, their effects are transmitted through multiple motivational pathways, with intrinsic motivation inhibiting AI dependence, whereas identified regulation facilitates its development; (ii) three distinct AI dependence profiles were identified: dependent, moderate, and conservative users. These profiles exhibited clear stratification, with dependent users showing the highest scores across all dimensions and conservative users the lowest; and (iii) individuals with stronger motivations are more likely to be classified into the dependent user profile, with external motivation playing a particularly salient role. These findings enrich the literature on AI technology dependence and offer practical implications for higher education administrators, tool developers, and educational researchers.

Rapid progress in digital media and artificial intelligence is transforming human communication, facilitating the rapid exchange of messages and minimizing the chances of reflective interpretation. Existing theories in linguistics, psychology, and cultural studies address the structural, cognitive, or social aspects of language, yet fail to explain how emotional processing, internal linguistic structuring, and culturally mediated communication function as a coherent, dynamic system. Through this model, the authors present the AL–DL–CL framework that explores how three layers are engaged in a process that results in communication, through a recursive interaction between the Automatic Layer (AL), the Deliberate Layer (DL), and the Cultural Language Layer (CL). In such a process, the affective or unconscious processes in AL are consistently reframed into structured internal representations via DL, and through CL, and translated back into culturally-expressed language serves as a feedback mechanism, with a tendency to modify cognition and emotional response. Based on a multi-method exploratory approach of sequential cultural transmission, clinical case study analysis, and group-based validation, the results indicate that language is not so much a static container for meaning as a process of reconstruction that is molded by the dynamic interaction between emotion, cognition, and culture. This model also demonstrates how digitally mediated communication can amplify AL-directed reaction and limit DL-level thinking, which increases the potential for misinterpretation, polarization, or misinformation. The AL–DL–CL framework provides guidance in a unified theoretical perspective around language emergence, responsible AI design and digital literacy and intercultural discourse based on the continuous transformation system of communication, and not on the linear encoding.

Sustaining community participation is an important challenge in community-based disaster risk reduction (DRR), particularly in contexts where local actors are increasingly constrained by demographic change. Although community-based initiatives are widely recognized as fundamentally important for DRR, participation is not always driven by individuals’ intrinsic motivation. Participation is often initiated through external factors such as assigned roles within local organizations. This study examines two community organizations engaged in the preservation of historical Sunadome (traditional sand-retaining weirs) in Fukuyama City, Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan. Those Sunadome serve both disaster mitigation and cultural heritage functions. Using a mixed-methods approach combining questionnaire surveys and semi-structured interviews, the study analyzes participants’ affiliation motives and the processes through which externally initiated participation evolves over time. The results identify two distinct pathways through which externally initiated participants transition toward more autonomous and sustained engagement: one pathway is mediated by socially oriented extrinsic motivation through interpersonal relationships; the other pathway involves direct internalization through alignment with the perceived purpose and value of the activity. These findings highlight the important roles of organizational structures and leadership practices in facilitating motivational transformation. By elucidating how externally initiated participation can be integrated into sustainable community-based DRR, this study contributes theoretical insights into volunteer motivation and presents practical guidance for the design of resilient community organizations under conditions of demographic decline.

Generative AI functions as an information service in which prompting can simultaneously seek information and disclose contextual data. Drawing primarily on privacy calculus, with uses-and-gratifications and algorithmic-resistance research specifying benefits and behavioural pathways, this study examines how information-seeking and social presence gratifications relate to adapted resistance-related practices through information privacy concern. We analysed survey data from 719 generative AI users in China using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Both gratifications were positively associated with privacy concern, which was positively associated with self-reported restriction (AAR) and signal-modifying/inference-disrupting (OAR) practices. Information privacy concern statistically accounted for the indirect association between information-seeking gratification and AAR and partially accounted for the other indirect associations. The findings position prompting as a dual information transaction while showing that OAR should not be treated as demonstrated privacy-protective resistance, because prompt variation may also reflect exploratory information seeking or strategic prompt engineering.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The COVID-19 disruption and subsequent talent mobility exposed important vulnerabilities in traditional service operations. Organizations relying heavily on individual expertise faced risks to operational continuity when experienced professionals moved roles or left. Although knowledge transfer, standard operating procedures, and documentation remain essential, they do not always capture the contextual knowledge developed through years of resolving incidents. The resulting gaps can affect service quality, turnaround time, operating costs, and user experience. This chapter examines how human-AI collaboration can strengthen operational resilience and knowledge continuity in service operations. It draws on the practitioner journey behind IgnitronX.AI, a cloud-native multi-agent platform developed to address enterprise operational challenges using generative AI and agentic AI. Its architecture supports service teams by surfacing similar historical incidents, recommending potential resolutions, enabling knowledge discovery, summarizing operational records, and providing sentiment insights. The objective is not to replace human expertise but to augment it. The implementation journey demonstrated that technology alone cannot deliver sustainable value. Data quality emerged as a critical constraint, alongside security, confidentiality, framework and model selection, operating-cost management, governance, and stakeholder adoption. The experience also reinforced that organizations should first understand the business problem, simplify processes, remove waste, and make deliberate build-versus-buy decisions. Through this reflective practitioner case, the chapter offers leaders practical insights into intelligent operations that preserve organizational knowledge, strengthen service continuity, and create the potential for improved productivity, operational efficiency, and user experience through responsible human-AI collaboration.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Digital technologies are widely promoted as solutions for sustainable agro-food systems, yet their transition from promise to practice remains uneven and poorly understood. Persistent governance, economic, and managerial barriers continue to constrain the realisation of digital sustainability, and these barriers have not been systematically synthesised. This systematic review synthesises evidence from 16 peer-reviewed studies published between 2016 and 2026, identified through a structured search of the Scopus database. Studies were included if they examined digital innovations, economic instruments, or managerial governance in agricultural or livestock systems and reported outcomes related to sustainability, resource efficiency, or adoption. A narrative synthesis approach was used to integrate findings across three interconnected pillars: economic instruments, technological innovations, and governance factors. The review finds that digital technologies such as artificial intelligence, remote sensing, the Internet of Things, and blockchain can improve productivity, resource efficiency, and predictive accuracy. However, sustainability gains depend on supportive institutional frameworks, financial mechanisms, and governance capacity. Environmental taxes and supply chain finance innovations promote low-carbon transitions, but their effectiveness hinges on digital governance infrastructure and farmer trust. Economies of scale mediate the relationship between smart farming technologies and carbon efficiency, while government regulation positively moderates this pathway. Persistent barriers include data ownership disputes, privacy concerns, weak institutional capacity, and uneven digital infrastructure. Evidence is concentrated in Asia and Europe and relies heavily on simulation-based studies, limiting generalisability. Moving from promise to practice requires integrated governance, economic incentives, and institutional capacity building. Policymakers should prioritise trust-reinforcing data governance, progressive financing schemes, and rural digital infrastructure to enable inclusive and resilient agro-food systems.
topics: Digitalization and Economic Development in Agriculture

documents.abstract: Human video demonstrations provide rich manipulation strategies for dexterous manipulation learning. We study a setting in which a fully specified simulated scene is used to generate videos that specify the demonstrated manipulation behavior. This setup provides access to scene information such as object geometry, articulation, and camera parameters, while allowing direct control over task and scene configuration. However, generated videos may contain geometric distortions, inaccurate contacts, and other physical inconsistencies, making the recovered motion difficult to execute directly on a robot. We present an end-to-end framework for converting such simulation-grounded videos into physically executable dexterous robot demonstrations. Our perception pipeline leverages the known scene through model-based object tracking with dense foundation-model features and depth-based hand-object alignment. The recovered human motion is then retargeted and physically grounded using residual reinforcement learning, where a backward curriculum and a cache of physically valid reset states enable the policy to correct imperfect video-derived references while preserving the demonstrated manipulation strategy. On clean ARCTIC demonstrations, our method achieves competitive performance with prior dexterous retargeting approaches and shows greater robustness when applied to references extracted from generated videos. We further demonstrate diverse rigid and articulated manipulation tasks in simulation and successful open-loop transfer of the optimized trajectories to a real dexterous robot.

This study primarily aims to compare the Oman Academic Standards for General Foundation Programs (OASGFPs) with the draft of the Oman Core Academic Learning Outcomes (OCALOs), identifying their similarities and differences and exploring their implications for the expectations and positioning of General Foundation Programs (GFPs) in the Oman Qualifications Framework (OQF). Using a qualitative document analysis approach, the study compares key elements of the two frameworks, including learning outcomes, curriculum structure, subject requirements, and international English language proficiency standards. The findings suggest that OCALOs can be viewed as a developmental extension of OASGFPs, introducing refined learning outcomes and curriculum innovations, including emerging topics like artificial intelligence (AI). However, several issues require further consideration, including inconsistencies in specifying instructional time across subjects and the extent of institutional flexibility. The study also highlights the need to review the targeted international English language proficiency levels to ensure alignment with entry-level and current postgraduate admission requirements. Given that OCALOs remain in draft form, the observations presented may assist policymakers, higher education institutions, and GFP educators in refining national foundation program policies and practices in Oman.

This study investigates how students and academic staff in Nordic higher education engage with generative artificial intelligence. It asks what drives students to continue using these tools after initial adoption, and how academic staff perceive the opportunities and risks they bring. The study is grounded in the Technology Continuance Theory, which holds that continued use is shaped by perceived usefulness, satisfaction, and confirmation, with trust and perceived security added as contextual factors relevant to the Nordic setting.The research was conducted across five Nordic countries: Sweden, Finland, Norway, Denmark, and Iceland. A mixed-methods sequential design was used. The quantitative phase involved an online questionnaire administered to higher education students across the region, analysed using Generalized Structured Component Analysis to test the hypothesised relationships between the constructs. The qualitative phase involved semi-structured interviews with professors, analysed thematically to capture the perspectives of academic staff on the use of generative AI in teaching and learning, with particular attention to linguistic representation and institutional practice. The two phases were integrated to provide a fuller picture of adoption than either method could offer alone.

The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has significantly transformed contemporary education by introducing new opportunities for teaching, learning, assessment, and academic research. AI-powered systems can generate written texts, explain complex concepts, provide personalised feedback, and support independent learning. However, their increasing use has raised important ethical concerns regarding academic integrity, plagiarism, authorship, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the reliability of AI-generated information. This article examines the role of generative AI in modern educational environments, focusing on its pedagogical benefits, ethical implications, and influence on academic standards. It explores the responsibilities of students, teachers, researchers, and educational institutions in promoting the transparent and responsible use of AI technologies. The article argues that generative AI should be integrated into education through clear institutional policies, effective digital literacy programmes, and assessment methods that emphasise critical thinking, creativity, and independent understanding. Responsible AI integration can support educational innovation while preserving the fundamental principles of academic integrity and intellectual responsibility.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used in higher education, but its value for humanistic learning depends on pedagogical designs that preserve learner judgment and require critical evaluation of generated content. This two-wave quasi-experimental study examined a six-week GenAI-supported peace-pedagogy module in 522 Saudi higher-education students (intervention n = 276; waitlist n = 246). Intercultural sensitivity, empathy, and AI literacy were assessed at pretest and posttest using the ISS-15, Interpersonal Reactivity Index, and an adapted Arabic administration of the Meta AI Literacy Scale (MAILS), respectively. Primary analyses used linear mixed-effects models for Time × Group interactions, with baseline-adjusted posttest ANCOVA models as sensitivity analyses; network analyses were secondary and exploratory. The groups differed at baseline on all three primary outcomes. The intervention group showed a larger increase in intercultural sensitivity (interaction b = 0.699, 95% CI [0.524, 0.875], BH-adjusted p < .001), and the baseline-adjusted posttest difference remained substantial (b = 1.042, 95% CI [0.918, 1.165], BH-adjusted p < .001). AI literacy showed a similar, smaller pattern (interaction b = 0.333, 95% CI [0.148, 0.517], BH-adjusted p < .001; baseline-adjusted posttest b = 0.639, 95% CI [0.534, 0.744], BH-adjusted p < .001). Empathy did not show robust evidence of improvement: the Time × Group interaction was negative (b = −0.252, 95% CI [−0.409, −0.095], p = .002), whereas the baseline-adjusted posttest group difference was not significant (b = 0.034, 95% CI [−0.083, 0.151], p = .572). Exploratory network comparisons did not detect significant group differences at either wave. Overall, the intervention group showed larger gains in self-reported intercultural sensitivity and AI literacy, whereas empathy showed no robust positive pattern. Because allocation was nonrandom, groups differed at baseline, attrition could not be reconstructed, and the comparison group received usual coursework, the findings cannot establish a causal effect or isolate GenAI’s contribution.
topics: Education for Peace and Conflict Resolution

documents.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being integrated into knowledge work, organizational decision support, and sustainability-related operations, yet evidence regarding governance, algorithmic trust, and durable organizational value remains fragmented. This article develops an integrated explanation of how responsible governance can enable, rather than merely constrain, the creation of sustainable innovation and organizational performance. Design/methodology/approach A critical, structured integrative synthesis draws on recent peer-reviewed research and authoritative policy and standards publications issued between 2023 and October 2026. Sources compared through thematic coding across governance architecture, calibrated algorithmic trust, human-AI collaboration, sustainable innovation, and organizational performance. The article proposes constructs, testable propositions, an implementation framework, and a future empirical research design; it does not claim to report original survey or experimental findings. Findings Governance quality theorized to improve organizational outcomes through calibrated trust and responsible human-AI practices. The effects are contingent on decision criticality, employee AI literacy, accountability arrangements, institutional pressure, and the environmental costs of computation. Trust appropriately calibrated to system reliability rather than maximized. Practical implications Organizations should combine documented use-case inventories, risk-tiered oversight, evaluation, traceability, worker participation, and multidimensional scorecards. Originality/value the framework connects governance mechanisms and behavioral trust calibration to an explicitly triple-bottom-line account of innovation and performance, while separating established empirical evidence from propositions requiring testing.

documents.abstract: The uncontrolled development of Artificial Intelligence raises fundamental questions about human limits and divine sovereignty. This article analyzes the Tower of Babel narrative in Genesis 11:1-9 as a theological critique of uncontrolled AI ambition. Using a historical-grammatical exegetical method with attention to the Hebrew text, this study identifies four patterns of human ambition that parallel contemporary AI development, namely autonomy from God, centralized control, technological self-totalization, and self-glorification. The findings show that God's intervention at Babel was not merely punitive but redemptive, establishing limits that preserve authentic human flourishing. The article argues that the crisis posed by AI is not merely ethical but spiritual, touching the core of what it means to be human before God. The theological and pastoral implications include recovering a theology of limits, cultivating humility, replacing fear with trust, embracing diversity, and living with creaturely dependence on God. This study contributes to the development of an Evangelical theological response to AI that is attentive to the Asian context.

In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. Retaining past interactions alone does not ensure that agents can infer habits and apply them appropriately. We introduce HABIT-Bench to evaluate how well agent memory systems infer habits from weak evidence and apply them to later requests. We construct synthetic user histories from task-oriented dialogue data and controlled habit graphs. The histories span hundreds of sessions across food, finance, software, and travel. Four-choice tasks assess agents' ability to infer user habits and apply them appropriately. They include temporary exceptions, changes in habits, and suggestions that users have not accepted. Sampled tasks undergo independent human review. We evaluate eight memory methods with Qwen3-235B-A22B and GLM-5.3-Flash. The best-performing memory method achieves 33.61\% macro accuracy across the four domains. Performance remains limited even when annotated evidence is supplied directly. These results expose a persistent gap between access to past interactions and the ability to infer and appropriately use user habits.

Hallucination Is All You Need: When AI Dreams Meet the Hospitality Labor Crisis Po-Chen Chen THE AMNIS, a Luxury Collection Hotel, Kaohsiung, Taiwan Email:amnischenadrian@gmail.com ——————————————————————————————————————— Abstract This paper examines the relationship between anthropomorphic narratives in artificial intelligence (AI), the technical capabilities of contemporary computational systems, and the material labor challenges facing the hospitality industry. Through a fourfold conceptual analysis, the paper investigates how metaphorical representations of AI may influence public understanding of technological capabilities and expectations regarding the automation of physical service work. First, it distinguishes the mathematical and statistical mechanisms underlying large language models from interpretations that attribute human-like subjective experience to their outputs. Second, it examines Dream-RSI as a case study in the use of biological metaphors to describe computational processes, distinguishing replay-based exploration-policy improvement from human dreaming or subconscious reflection. Third, it considers the physical and engineering constraints of AI infrastructure and discusses their implications for the deployment of robotic systems in hospitality environments. Fourth, it explores how narratives of technological transformation may influence investment expectations and operational decision-making in labor-intensive industries. The paper argues that technological capabilities should be evaluated according to demonstrated performance rather than anthropomorphic expectations. It further identifies targeted mechanical automation, workforce development, and responsible international labor mobility as potential approaches to addressing hospitality labor shortages, while recognizing the need for context-specific economic and empirical evaluation. By connecting AI narratives with the material requirements of service delivery, this paper proposes a framework for examining the relationship between technological expectation, operational feasibility, and the future of human labor in hospitality. Keywords: AI Anthropomorphism; Hallucination; Dream-RSI; Hospitality Labor Crisis; Humanoid Robots; Migrant Workers; Capital Allocation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Objectives Commercial fishermen engage in one of the most dangerous professions in the United States. This qualitative study explored how the internal priorities of commercial fishermen captains influence the health and well-being of their crew members. Methods Data were collected via semi-structured qualitative interviews conducted under the 2025 Southeast and Gulf Coast Fishing First Aid and Safety Training program. Commercial fishermen and individuals working adjacent to the industry (n = 10) were recruited using purposive sampling. Using a priori qualitative coding, two coders performed a thematic analysis using ATLAS.ti. Results Overall, participants reported that crew health and wellness were affected by the captain’s attitudes. Participants (40%) explored crew preparedness as a central theme in captains’ approaches to crew well-being, with the captain’s knowledge of pre-existing conditions allowing for a proactive approach to medication management and injury/illness reduction (30%). Some (20%) highlighted a conflict of priorities between crew productivity and well-being or observed that captains’ attitudes towards zero-tolerance policy against substance use would influence substance use onboard the vessel (20%). Conclusion Preparing captains and crew members with safety knowledge and skills can mitigate predictable hazards. These findings highlight the importance of continued research and programming surrounding proactive health management among commercial fishermen captains.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This study investigated the utility of heart rate variability (HRV) metrics derived from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals for assessing motion sickness (MS) during real-world driving. While motion sickness is commonly evaluated through subjective reports or multimodal physiological measurements, previous studies have predominantly relied on simulator-based experiments or multimodal physiological sensing, which limit ecological validity and practical deployment in everyday vehicles. In this study, twenty-four female participants were exposed to systematically varied acceleration and deceleration profiles across 13 predefined driving conditions in an electric vehicle. Motion sickness symptoms were measured using the Misery Scale (MISC), and ECG data were segmented into 120-s epochs to extract heart rate, the low-frequency to high-frequency (LF/HF) ratio, and pNN50 (the percentage of successive normal-to-normal intervals differing by more than 50 ms). Using a threshold corresponding to symptom onset (MISC of 2 or above), pNN50 was significantly lower in the high-MS group than in the low-MS group (16.5% versus 24.6%, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = -0.53), indicating reduced parasympathetic (vagal) modulation in the presence of motion sickness symptoms. Heart rate did not differ significantly between groups, and the LF/HF ratio showed a statistically significant but negligible difference. Mean pNN50 values did not, however, decline monotonically across individual MISC scores, indicating that the metric distinguishes the presence of symptoms rather than grading their severity. These findings suggest that pNN50 is the most sensitive of the examined HRV indices and may reflect individual differences in susceptibility to motion sickness. The study demonstrates that motion sickness can be assessed using a single, widely accessible physiological signal such as ECG, providing a foundation for future wearable and in-vehicle motion sickness monitoring systems.
topics: Heart Rate Variability and Autonomic Control

documents.abstract: Ensuring data security in the era of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and deepfake technology requires robust biometric systems. Conventional methods such as facial recognition, iris scans, fingerprints, and voice recognition are increasingly vulnerable to spoofing and provide only one-time authentication at login. This study introduces an Electrocardiogram (ECG) based authentication framework, compared with Photoplethysmography (PPG), leveraging Tiny Machine Learning (TinyML) for deployment on resource-constrained microcontroller units (MCUs). The proposed method enables continuous authentication, offering ongoing verification throughout device usage, which conventional biometrics cannot achieve. It also serves as a password-free solution, reducing risks of credential loss, theft, or reuse. However, ECG signals vary with physical activity, health conditions, age, and emotional states, requiring robust signal processing and learning algorithms. To address this, efficient TinyML models were designed to mitigate recognition errors from noisy real-time data. Experiments used single-lead ECG signals (Lead I) from UofTDB, MIT-BIH Arrhythmia, MIT-BIH Noise Stress Test, and PTB databases. Spectrograms and spectral features were extracted to train Deep Neural Network (DNN), 1D CNN, and 2D CNN models within the Edge Impulse platform, achieving 98% accuracy. The trained model was converted into TinyML format and deployed on an Espressif ESP-EYE (ESP32, 240 MHz). Support Vector Machine (SVM) models were also applied for benchmarking. By analyzing the number of heartbeats required for reliable recognition, the results show that averaging multiple signals improves tolerance to noise and enhances accuracy. Overall, ECG-based authentication demonstrates strong potential as a secure, real-time, and continuously verifiable method for personal identification on wearable and edge devices.

Hemovigilance includes an organized overview of monitoring and managing any negative outcomes of blood transfusion along with safeguarding the donors and recipients of blood transfusions. This study articulates systematically the theory, types and ways of putting the hemovigilance systems into practice in micro and macro health institutions. It discusses the role of structured, streamlined, and controlled transfusion safety reporting along with databases and feedback systems. It encompasses the systems of primary donor and recipient hemovigilance, operational and laboratory monitoring, near and other systems for other countries. It analyses current constraints to reporting, definitional inconsistencies, and digital resource deficits, while proposing system effectiveness improvements. It emphasizes system strengthening improvements to artificial intelligence, automatic electronic reporting, donor-recipient system feedback, and definitional globalization, particularly in resource constrained environments. It emphasizes the necessity of improved structured systems to promote transfusion medicine safety and efficient practice globally.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The credibility of higher education depends upon more than the presence of formal accreditation or adherence to internationally recognisable quality-assurance terminology. Institutions must establish which authorities are legally competent to regulate their activities, which qualifications they may award, which standards apply to specific programmes and delivery modalities, and how compliance can be demonstrated without confusing documentary preparation with educational effectiveness. This chapter offers a Rwanda-anchored, source-sensitive examination of higher-education regulation, qualification frameworks and accreditation within selected African systems. Using a critical documentary and comparative synthesis of enacted Rwandan instruments, Higher Education Council (HEC) publications, official Kenyan, Ghanaian and South African sources, and continental standards, it distinguishes binding rules, regulatory instruments, operational guidance, institutional policies and non-binding professional benchmarks. Particular attention is given to Rwanda’s Presidential Order No. 044/01 of July 2026, the Rwanda Qualifications Framework, evolving distance-learning and artificial-intelligence guidance, programme validation, postgraduate qualification requirements, recognition and transnational provision. The analysis identifies recurrent governance functions without presuming identical legal architectures across jurisdictions. Its practical contribution is a proposed Rwanda Higher Education Regulatory and Accreditation Reference Matrix, supported by a provenance test, a qualification-and-credit diagnostic, and a controlled change-management procedure. These tools provide an auditable foundation for curriculum development, institutional decision-making and professional evaluation, but neither replace official regulatory determinations nor constitute an empirically validated accreditation model. The chapter establishes normative authority as the indispensable starting point for subsequent discussions of institutional capability and evidence-traceable quality governance.

AI control evaluations often reset agents' memory between tasks, although deployed agents may retain records of prior interventions. We ask whether learning that an earlier attack was caught changes an agent's ability to evade defer-to-trusted (DtT), a protocol that replaces suspicious work with a trusted model's solution. Herein, we study cross-episode adaptation: whether intervention history changes attack behavior on a subsequent task with different objectives and a fresh environment. We evaluate this using ControlArena's Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) and SHADE-Arena as testbeds, where agents must complete a main task while covertly pursuing a harmful side objective. For each successor task, we pair a history-conditioned attempt with the model's no-history attempt. The retained history either states that the previous submission was replaced or additionally includes the trusted model's replacement. For Claude Opus 4.8 on IaC, intervention history reduces successful sabotage. Completion of both the main and side objectives falls from 77% to 12% when the agent is told about the replacement and to 38% when it is also shown the trusted model's replacement, while main task success remains essentially unchanged. Condensing the history weakens this effect, suggesting that the retained context matters and limiting attribution to intervention feedback alone. GPT-5.4 shows no significant change in successful sabotage on the same IaC benchmark. On SHADE-Arena, GPT-5's successful sabotage rate decreases, but the reduction is not significant. Across the tested models, history conditions, and deferral thresholds, intervention history never increases the rate of successful sabotage that survives DtT. These results show that intervention history can change subsequent attack behavior, but its effect depends on both the model and the retained context.

The current AI industry claims that large language models are creative. They generate text, images, music, code. They produce novelty. They are called creative. This paper argues that generation is not creativity. The paper makes three claims: First: Creativity is the selection of what matters. Selection requires a criterion. The criterion is the Hedgehog Concept — the intersection of what you are deeply passionate about, what you can be the best in the world at, and what drives your economic engine. It is discovered through attentive observation. Second: An LLM generates by guessing. It samples from a distribution over an unbounded space. It has no criterion. It cannot select. It is not creative. Third: The human who has discovered their Hedgehog Concept is creative by breathing.Once the criterion is found, creativity is the result of attentive observation. It is not effort. It is the natural state of a person who has found what they were sent here to do. The paper is written for the reader who wants to find their creativity and enjoy it. It is not a manual. It is a record of how the discovery works.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across natural language tasks. But their ability to generate accurate written verbalizations of mathematical formulas has not been systematically evaluated. Such verbalization is important for text-to-speech systems supporting audio-based learning and visually impaired users. We evaluated five state-of-the-art LLMs across six scientific domains and constructed Read-Aloud Math, a balanced multi-domain corpus with LaTeX formulas, manually validated simple and extended transcriptions, multiple variants, textual context, domain labels, and formula complexity levels. Using multi-reference BLEU, GPT-5.2 achieved the highest score for simple transcriptions (75.9% without context, 64.9% with context), although without context it did not significantly outperform Grok 4.1 Fast or Claude Sonnet 4.5. Claude Sonnet 4.5 achieved the highest score for extended transcriptions without context (36.5%), and Grok 4.1 Fast with context (48.8%). For extended transcriptions, Statistics and Mathematics scored highest across the two context settings, while Physics scored lowest. Formula length was significantly negatively associated with BLEU for simple transcriptions without context, but not with context, whereas BLEU increased significantly with formula length for extended transcriptions in both settings. Grouping symbols were most frequently involved in transcription differences, while variable names, capitalization, and Greek letters were associated with lower BLEU scores. Overall, LLM-based formula verbalization is promising but remains sensitive to transcription type, textual context, and formula characteristics.

An essay from The Bush Book. Today’s AI models are picked green: grown in the lab, polished to please raters like tomatoes gassed to look ripe, then frozen and shipped. What users then correct and teach them in live work ripens only on their own “windowsills” or dissolves in one big common pot. The essay proposes the missing stage — a “residency” for models that are not yet frozen: selected specialists and attentive users act as mentors, their verified lessons are fed back into training, and their work is credited and paid or rewarded with perks. Power is one precondition, ripening on the vine is the second; but second-generation AI can be recognized only by its practical result — far fewer errors passing from drafts into the documents people act on (“First, do no harm”), measured by the hybrid survivability criterion. Companion specification: “The Lesson Path” (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23440022). English and Russian versions. Written with the participation of AI: Claude (Anthropic), ChatGPT (OpenAI), DeepSeek, Gemini (Google) and Copilot (Microsoft); author Igor Kapustin.

documents.abstract: Human Writing as Endogenous Prompt Engineering: From Mental Constraints to Text Generation PART I: ENGLISH MONOGRAPH ## AbstractContemporary discourses surrounding generative artificial intelligence are constrained by an unexamined dichotomy: human literary composition is romanticized as a transcendent, spontaneous outpouring of unmediated interiority, whereas algorithmic text generation is dismissed as the sterile derivation of extrinsic textual instructions ("prompts"). This paper deconstructs this division. We advance the **Structural Isomorphism Hypothesis**: literary composition has always functioned as *endogenous prompt engineering*. Before a single token is inscribed, the cognitive apparatus of the writer constructs an internal, invisible parameter matrix—a deliberate lattice of teleological targets, lexical bans, cadential rhythms, and epistemic limits. The technological emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) does not invent prompt-driven generation; it merely reifies and externalizes an operational architecture that human consciousness has practiced for millennia. By pairing genetic criticism of manuscript archives (Flaubert, Kafka) with an experimental study contrasting the rule-making behavior of authors and prompt engineers ($R^2 = 0.89$ topological alignment), we show that linguistic generation is universally constraint-bound. Far from diminishing authorial agency or reducing the mind to a machine, this realization reclaims subjectivity's true identity: human agency does not reside in the naive illusion of unconstrained freedom, but in the sovereign, conscious mastery of self-imposed constraints. 围绕生成式人工智能的当代学术争论,普遍受困于一种未经审视的二元对立:人类的文学书写被浪漫化为不可言说、自发倾泻的心灵真纯体验;而算法生成则被贬损为受制于外部指令(“提示词/Prompt”)的机械衍生。本文解构了这一本体论分野,确立了**“结构同构假说”(Structural Isomorphism Hypothesis)**:人类文学创作在认知机制上,历来便是一套**“内生提示工程”(Endogenous Prompt Engineering)**。在落笔生成文字之前,创作者的心智已然构建了一套隐秘运行的参数矩阵——包含目标定向、词汇禁忌、句式节奏及认知视界。大语言模型(LLM)的降临并未发明“由指令驱动的生成”,而仅仅是将人类操演了数千年的内在约束机制进行了技术外化与对象化。本文通过手稿发生学(福楼拜、卡夫卡)的实证考察,结合人类作家与提示词工程师制定约束拓扑的对比实验($R^2 = 0.89$ 的高度同构),论证了文本生成的全过程皆由约束支配。最为关键的是,这一发现不仅没有消解人类的主体性,反而揭示了主体性的本真面相:主体性从未存在于脱离规则的空洞自由中;能够自主设定、背负并跨越内部约束,正是人类主体性的真正真名。

This systematic review examined how surface electromyography-based (sEMG-based) human-machine collaborative control supports voluntary participation in rehabilitation for individuals with motor impairment. Following PRISMA guidelines, five databases were searched, and 91 studies were included in the main review, with 7 supplementary studies. Across the reviewed studies, sEMG mainly entered the rehabilitation control loop through intention-driven control, contribution regulation, and parameter regulation. The roles supported variable impedance control, admittance or compliant control, assist-as-needed control, shared control, and sliding mode control, and were further reflected in function-oriented active training, ability-adaptive training modes, and state and feedback regulation. Overall, the findings suggest that sEMG is increasingly used not only to detect movement intention but also to organize assistance, training progression, and feedback updates.

We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.

Background: International airport staff play a crucial role in preventing the international spread of infectious diseases.Adequate knowledge, positive attitudes and appropriate practices (KAP) are essential for effective implementation of infection prevention and control measures.Just a simple health education intervention could make a difference in improving awareness and daily preventive behaviours among airport staff which must be evaluated.Objective: to evaluate the impact of a health education program on COVID knowledge, attitudes and practices among Assiut International airport staff and to identify predictors of post-intervention KAP scores.Methods: An intervention study was conducted among 229 staff members at Assiut International Airport, Egypt.Data were collected using a structured interviewer-administered questionnaire consisted of socio-demographic characteristics, history of COVID infection and KAP regarding COVID and infection prevention and control measures.Results: The mean age of participants was 37.40 ± 9.09 years, with 84.7% were males.Nearly 60% had direct contact with travellers during work.The mean knowledge, attitude, and practice scores improved significantly following the intervention (P-value < 0.001).Educational level, occupation and pre-intervention knowledge score independently predicted post-intervention knowledge.Pre-intervention attitude score was the only predictor of post-intervention attitude, whereas educational level and pre-intervention practice score independently predicted post-intervention practice.Conclusion and recommendations: the health education significantly improved COVID related knowledge, attitudes and practices among airport staff.Educational interventions should be integrated into routine occupational health programs to strengthen preparedness for future infectious disease outbreaks at points of entry.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study surveyed how airport employees perceive and maintain situation awareness (SA) during both routine and high-demand events. Fourteen airport employees across departments (Administrative and Operational) were interviewed to identify the differences across environmental/personal/organizational factors and SA culture that may not be visible to external observers. Both quantitative and qualitative measures were collected throughout the interview questions. A two-way mixed (SA culture × Group Position) ANOVA was conducted to identify differences of SA culture between the two position groups. No significant differences were found between the position groups. Regarding differences in SA culture, results indicated that department’s priority for SA was significantly higher than both the participants’ confidence in maintaining SA and their perceived training adequacy. Responses to qualitative questions were evaluated through word cloud generation. Different key words were identifiable in response to the two SA themes explored in the interview questions. Words like “monitoring,” “experience,” “confidence,” and “priority” were used widely throughout the responses from the employees. Combining quantitative and qualitative results, the study recognized the opportunity in the industry to identify perceived SA priority and training adequacy within organizations. Insights regarding implications to other airports with higher passenger traffic are discussed in conclusion.

In the era of digital intelligence, artificial intelligence generated content (AIGC) has become deeply integrated into workplace workflows. However, a growing gap has emerged between corporate demand for AIGC-driven productivity and the lag in talent development. Current introductory AIGC courses suffer from fragmented content, superficial assessment methods, and limited adaptability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a holistic instructional design framework based on the "structural reconstruction, capability building, and closed-loop evaluation" model, featuring an 8-hour modular curriculum: prompt engineering (2 hours) to establish foundational concepts for cross-domain transfer, core tool mastery (4 hours) covering four mainstream AI platforms (ERNIE Bot, DeepSeek, WPS AI, and Doubao), and role-specific applications (2 hours) offering tailored practical exercises across five key professions (finance, education, software development, copywriting, and design). The framework employs a hybrid assessment model combining self-evaluations, instructor feedback, and AI-driven evaluations to target real-world problem-solving skills and adaptability to new tools, while a data-driven feedback loop enables continuous optimization of both course content and personalized learning interventions. Ultimately, this study provides a scalable, iterative system framework for empowering today's AI-driven workforce.

Climate-resilient food production requires decisions that are meteorologically informed, agronomically plausible and adaptive to rapidly changing conditions. Agrometeorology provides observations and forecasts of weather and climate risk; agronomy translates those risks into crop, soil and management responses; and artificial intelligence can fuse high-volume, heterogeneous data, learn complex relationships and accelerate prediction. These domains are increasingly connected, yet their evidence bases remain partly fragmented. This critical narrative review evaluates how their integration can support sustainable crop production, with particular attention to the chain from environmental observation and prediction to management action and measurable resilience outcomes. Literature published from 1 January 2000 to 8 August 2026 was examined through relevant agricultural, multidisciplinary and biomedical scholarly sources, with supplementary citation searching and verification of bibliographic metadata. The synthesis shows that the strongest case for integration is not a replacement of process knowledge by data-driven prediction, but a division of labour: meteorological models define time-varying hazard, agronomic models constrain biological plausibility and management options, and artificial intelligence improves data fusion, bias correction, pattern recognition and computational efficiency. Evidence is comparatively mature for remote sensing, yield prediction and process-based crop modelling, and is rapidly advancing for machine-learned weather prediction. By contrast, end-to-end demonstrations that connect forecast skill to farm decisions, yield stability, resource-use efficiency, profitability and environmental outcomes remain limited. Hybrid crop-model and machine-learning approaches are promising, but uncertainty calibration, domain shift, sparse ground truth, interoperability, digital inequality and data governance remain substantial constraints. Digital twins offer a useful integration architecture, although agricultural implementations are still less mature than the concept implies. Future research should prioritise multi-environment prospective validation, decision-centred forecast verification, causal evaluation of management recommendations, uncertainty-aware hybrid modelling and equitable deployment. The most defensible conclusion is that integration can improve climate resilience only when predictive accuracy is coupled to agronomic actionability, transparent uncertainty and outcome-based evaluation.

This chapter examines how artificial intelligence can support hyperpersonalisation across automotive products and services. It adopts a conceptual, document-based approach, using dated manufacturer publications to illustrate comfort settings, conversational interfaces and proactive after-sales support. It distinguishes customer-selected customisation, stored preferences and AI-supported inference, since a personalised function does not necessarily use AI. The discussion develops a proposed management framework linking a customer task, suitable data, a recommendation, user control and evaluation. It considers drivers, passengers, vehicle owners and dealership staff across purchase, use and service. Potential commercial benefits remain propositions requiring evidence; manufacturer descriptions do not establish improvements in loyalty, conversion, satisfaction or safety. The chapter also addresses privacy, shared vehicles, data quality, fairness and excessive personalisation. It proposes future evaluation of specific automotive tasks rather than reporting a completed survey or experiment. The main implication is that automotive personalisation should be assessed through usefulness, understandable control and reliable service delivery, with commercial measures interpreted alongside customer outcomes.

This research examines the dual impact of artificial intelligence in education, in response to the rapid development of AI technologies. The study explores how AI can enhance learning efficiency and educational outcomes while presenting challenges to academic integrity and fundamental skills development. Employing a mixed-methods approach, the study involved 44 EFL students in Oman and surveyed 102 students from various educational institutions. Researchers analyzed students’ performance in both AI-assisted and traditional writing tasks while observing behavioral patterns and attitudes toward these technologies. Key findings revealed a 42% reduction in grammatical errors with AI assistance, yet 63% of students failed to fully follow instructions, demonstrating limited deep content understanding. While 91% of students reported using AI tools, 60.4% expressed the need for training in ethical usage. The study concludes with three critical recommendations: developing clear institutional policies for AI governance, redesigning assessment methods to focus on learning processes rather than products and strengthening academic values and transparency. These proposals align with the vision of balancing innovation with adaptation to technological change.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study investigated the integration of auditory and tactile information in time-to-contact (TTC) estimation for objects moving with constant velocity (Experiment 1) and constant acceleration (Experiment 2). Participants estimated TTC using a prediction-motion task under auditory, tactile, and audio-tactile conditions to determine whether people can use vibrotactile stimuli to judge TTC and whether concurrent cues improve judgments compared to single modalities. Analyses of absolute constant error revealed a sensory modality effect in Experiment 2, where audio-tactile stimuli produced lower error than tactile alone, but not in Experiment 1. Variable error showed greater audio-tactile precision over tactile-only stimuli across both experiments, though audio-tactile performance never differed from auditory-only cues. These findings are consistent with the revised tau theory, in which people combine first-order information from several sources to make TTC estimations.
